books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924

stimulus.text: “One of the rights which the freeman has always guarded with most jealous care is that of enjoying the rewards of his own industry. . . . A government which lays taxes on the people not required by urgent public necessity and sound public policy is not a protector of liberty, but an instrument of tyranny.” — President Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain.
stimulus.source_note: Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain (pre-1930). Text per the American Presidency Project.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Calvin Coolidge, address 'Economy in the Interest of All,' June 30, 1924, public domain
stem: Coolidge's argument in the passage rests on the belief that

options.text: the government should manage the economy to prevent downturns
options.misconception: Coolidge argues the opposite. He says government should take only what urgent need requires, not manage the economy.

options.text: taxes beyond urgent public needs threaten individual freedom
prosperity depends on high tariffs on imported goods
options.misconception: Coolidge says nothing about tariffs here. His argument is about taxes and the right to enjoy one's property.

options.text: the Constitution gives Congress power to tax without limit
options.misconception: Coolidge says the opposite: the power to tax is the power to destroy, and the Constitution guards it carefully.

rationales.A: Coolidge calls a government that taxes beyond urgent need an instrument of tyranny, not a manager of the economy.
rationales.B: Coolidge says the freeman guards the rewards of his own industry, and calls taxation beyond urgent public necessity a threat to freedom itself.
rationales.C: Background from the books: tariffs were a separate 1920s debate, and Coolidge's passage argues about taxation, not trade.
rationales.D: Coolidge says the Constitution requires revenue bills to start in the House precisely because the taxing power is dangerous and must be guarded.
rationales.general:
1. Find Coolidge's core claim: a freeman must enjoy the rewards of his own industry.
2. Find his warning: the power to tax is the power to destroy.
3. Put them together: taxes beyond urgent need take that freedom away.
4. His argument rests on taxes threatening freedom when they go too far.
Remember: a speech about taxes argues from a right, so find the right it defends.
